summary:
Analog Atlas is a web platform that helps scientists find and verify places on Earth that resemble target sites on the Moon and Mars. NASA tests rovers, instruments and crews at these analog sites, but candidate sites are chosen from coarse satellite data, and checking them means costly field trips.

A researcher picks a lunar or Martian target. Our model compares it with all 92,172 land areas on Earth using NASA data (MODIS, NASA POWER, LOLA and MOLA) and produces a similarity heatmap. Each score explains what matches, what differs and what is only estimated. In testing, known analog sites rank in the top 1%.

For a shortlisted site, the researcher sends a verification request with a simulated rover walkthrough on real terrain and questions drafted from the weakest data. Local contributors answer with photos and observations tied to coordinates or video timestamps. A reviewer accepts or rejects each one, building an evidence record that helps scientists correct their data.
details:
What it does

Analog Atlas helps scientists find places on Earth that resemble a target site on the Moon or Mars, and then verify those places with the people who know them. NASA tests rovers, instruments and crews at such “analog sites”, but candidate sites are usually chosen from coarse satellite data, and checking them means sending people into the field.

How it works

  1. Pick a target. There are eight built-in targets (for example lunar maria, the lunar south pole, Gale crater on Mars), or any point on the Moon can become a custom target.
  2. Score all of Earth. Our model compares the target with every one of Earth’s 92,172 land cells across nine groups of properties: rock type, aridity, temperature, landforms, vegetation, soil chemistry, regolith, altitude and albedo. The results appear as a heatmap on a 3D globe.
  3. Explain every score. Each place gets a breakdown of what matches, what differs, and how much of the score rests on measurements versus estimates.
  4. Verify locally. For a shortlisted site, the researcher creates a verification request. It includes a simulated rover walkthrough on real terrain and specific questions, drafted automatically from the weakest data. Local contributors answer “Matches”, “Differs” or “Cannot judge”, with photos and sources tied to coordinates or video timestamps.
  5. Review. The researcher accepts, rejects or asks for more evidence. Accepted observations build the site’s evidence record; they never silently change the score.

Benefits and impact

  • Lower cost. Volunteer ground checks cost about 92% less per point than professional field surveys (€2.60 vs €32.40, Laso Bayas et al. 2020). A year of running the platform (about $340) costs less than the daily expenses alone of one two-person field visit.
  • Better data. Contributions show scientists where global datasets are wrong or too coarse. For example, the known Mars analog Río Tinto scores only 5% because its acid river is invisible in a 50 km data cell.
  • Fewer wasted trips. Scientists travel only to sites that have passed local checks, which also avoids around 2.3 tonnes of CO₂ per person for each long-haul flight not taken.
  • A role for local experts. Geologists, guides and students get a direct way to contribute to Moon and Mars research.

Tools and technologies

  • Interface: TypeScript and React with Vite; CesiumJS for the 3D Earth, Moon and Mars globes.
  • Rover simulator: three.js, with NASA’s Perseverance and Curiosity 3D models, real Copernicus 30 m terrain, and a drive model run at Earth, Mars or Moon gravity.
  • Data pipeline: Node.js scripts that rebuild every dataset from its source.
  • NASA data: MODIS (surface temperature, vegetation), NASA POWER (precipitation, water vapour, pressure, UV, albedo), LRO LOLA and the LROC mare map (Moon), MGS MOLA (Mars), NASA Moon Trek, Mars Trek and GIBS (imagery).
  • Partner and other open data: Copernicus DEM (ESA), the GLiM rock map, and the Smithsonian volcano database.
  • Hardware: none beyond our laptops. Everything runs in a web browser.

What makes it creative

Tools for finding analog sites and citizen-science projects both exist, but they are separate today. Analog Atlas joins them in one loop: a whole-Earth similarity map, explained scores, and reviewed local evidence that feeds back to the scientist. The rover walkthrough lets someone who knows a valley spot what the satellite reconstruction got wrong, without needing any scientific background.

What our team considered

  • Honesty. Every value is labelled as measured, mapped or estimated. Gravity, atmosphere and radiation are listed but never scored. The rover simulator is labelled as a screening tool, not validated physics.
  • Trust. Contributions are reviewed before they count, and they never change scores automatically.
  • Cost and sustainability. The scoring and the simulator run on the user’s own device. The planned shared backend would cost about $28 a month at pilot scale.
  • Reproducibility. Every dataset can be rebuilt from open sources with one command.
  • Current limits. Requests are stored in the browser for now, and a shared backend with accounts and moderation is the next step. The model also cannot see features smaller than about 50 km, which is exactly why local verification exists.
